doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: Writing, criticism and the jazz business
title: The critic's function and other roles in the jazz industry
summary: Thomas explains the critic as go-between for musicians and public, and the business jobs that support the music, which Rowe thinks are done better by musicians.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: But I mean there’s a function for that. There’s a critical function which basically is the go-between between the musicians and the public. Now some musicians would say we don’t need that. I mean the public, if they hear it then they can form their own impression. Well sometimes they might not hear it unless there is some vehicles,

publications, individuals, who are promoting it, publicizing it, you know letting folks know. So the critical function is to take those, you know the artist’s intent plus the codes and standards and traditions of the particular art form, and then translate all of that in a way that a general layperson can understand it and relate to it, and hopefully connect with it. I mean that’s the critical function I think. So it serves a purpose. But getting back to my other point, I mean there are people you need on the business side. You need people to own venues. You need people to manage artists. You have venues that have their own functions that are played in a venue. There are so many levels. So there’s a lot that can be done, you know. If you go on to law school you can do entertainment law, you know, and help out. So there’s all kinds of ways of being involved with the music and continuing to support it, other than just by being a working musician.
Yeah. And I’d like to think that the people in those positions do better at it if they were musicians, or if they are musicians.

I would think so. Because there’s a certain sensitivity that you have. There’s a certain appreciation that you have, of what it actually takes to become good at playing an instrument. And it takes devotion and dedication, like anything. But you’re talking about something that, there’s a learning curve to it.
